cases.question: What happens during a Kafka consumer group rebalance, and what does it cost the application?
rubric_key_points: A rebalance is triggered when group membership or the subscribed partitions change (a member joins, leaves, or is judged dead)
Partitions are reassigned among the members that remain, coordinated by the group coordinator
Under the eager protocol, consumption stops for the whole group while this happens
Offsets not committed before partitions are revoked lead to messages being processed again
Cooperative (incremental) rebalancing or static membership reduce how much is paused
cases.model_answer: A rebalance starts when a consumer joins or leaves the group, or stops sending heartbeats and is judged dead, or when the partitions of a subscribed topic change. The group coordinator has the members rejoin and partitions are reassigned among them. With the eager protocol every member gives up all its partitions first, so the whole group stops consuming until the new assignment arrives. Anything processed but not committed before revocation is processed again by the new owner. Cooperative rebalancing moves only the partitions that need to move, and static membership avoids a rebalance when a member restarts quickly.
cases.candidate_answer: A rebalance happens when the group's membership changes: a consumer joins, leaves, or misses heartbeats and the coordinator decides it is dead. It also happens if the topic's partitions change. The group coordinator makes everyone rejoin and the partitions get reassigned across whoever is left. With the default eager protocol every consumer revokes all its partitions first, so the whole group stops consuming until assignment finishes. If a consumer had processed messages but not committed the offsets when its partitions were revoked, the new owner reads from the last committed offset and those messages are processed twice. You can reduce the pause with cooperative rebalancing, which only moves the partitions that have to move, or with static membership so a quick restart does not trigger one.

In my experience it is really critical to think carefully about consumer groups because they are fundamental to how Kafka achieves scalability. cases.question: Why would you add an index to a database table, and when would you decide not to?
rubric_key_points: An index lets the database find matching rows without scanning the whole table
It speeds up reads that filter, join, or sort on the indexed columns
Every insert, update, and delete has to maintain the index, so writes get slower
An index takes storage, and one on a column with few distinct values or on a small table may not be used at all
cases.model_answer: An index is a separate structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database go straight to the rows matching a condition instead of reading every row. It helps queries that filter, join, or sort on those columns. The cost is that every write has to update the index as well, and the index takes space. On a small table, or a column with only a few distinct values, the planner may ignore it, so it costs writes and buys nothing.
cases.candidate_answer: An index lets the database jump to the matching rows instead of scanning the whole table, so queries that filter, join, or order by that column get faster. The price is on writes: every insert, update, and delete has to update the index too. It also uses disk. I would skip it on a small table or on a column with very few distinct values, like a boolean, because the planner will probably not use it and you pay the write cost for nothing.
